passage: Thomas had four hours to submit a market report to a client in Nairobi, and the office printer and half the network were down. He used an AI writing tool to draft the summary from his data. It was fast and fluent. His colleague Pallavi glanced at it. "That growth figure looks odd." Thomas checked: the tool had made up a number that wasn't in his data. His stomach dropped. With the clock ticking, he went through every figure, line by line, against the spreadsheet. Two more were wrong. He fixed them and added a note that AI had helped draft the text but he had verified the numbers. He sent it with twenty minutes to spare. He told Pallavi, "I owe you tea."

qa.q: What did the AI tool make up in the report?
qa.a: It made up a growth figure that wasn't in his data.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when he found the made-up number?
qa.a: He felt a jolt of fear, as his stomach dropped, realising he'd almost sent false data.

qa.q: What did Thomas do right under time pressure?
qa.a: He checked every figure against the spreadsheet, fixed errors and was open about using AI while staying responsible for the numbers.

qa.q: What would have happened if Pallavi hadn't glanced at the report?
qa.a: The client might have received false figures, damaging trust in Thomas and his firm.

grounding: Shows a young professional using AI under pressure while verifying results and keeping accountability.

passage: Sahil, a junior developer at a Pune software firm, had started using an AI assistant to write most of his code. His team lead, Pankaj, noticed Sahil's pull requests getting bigger and faster. One afternoon Pankaj asked him to explain a function line by line. Sahil couldn't. His ears went red. "The AI wrote it," he mumbled. Pankaj didn't scold him. "Use it, it's useful. But if you can't explain it, you can't own it." They agreed that Sahil would write core logic himself each Friday, and use AI for tests and boilerplate. He would also review every AI suggestion before committing. After a month, Sahil caught an AI bug in someone else's code during review. He felt proud.

qa.q: On which day would Sahil write core logic himself?
qa.a: He would write it himself each Friday.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when he couldn't explain the function?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed; his ears went red and he mumbled his answer.

qa.q: What balance did Sahil and Pankaj agree on?
qa.a: Sahil would use AI for tests and boilerplate, write core logic himself on Fridays and review every AI suggestion.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see the AI assistant?
qa.a: He sees it as a useful tool but insists the developer must understand and own the code it produces. 👍

grounding: Shows a young developer learning to delegate to AI while keeping accountability and protecting his own skills.

passage:
"Sudha-di, look. I made the whole school newsletter in ten minutes with the AI tool!"
"Ten minutes? Hansa, did you read it?"
"Mostly. Why?"
"Because it says the annual day is on the fifteenth. It's on the twelfth."
"Oh no. It must have guessed."
"And this quote from the principal. Did she say that?"
"...I don't think so."
"So it made it up."
"I just wanted to save time. I have forty copies to print tonight."
"Save time, fine. But your name's on it, not the tool's."
"So I check every fact?"
"Every date, every name, every quote. And write the principal's message yourself. You're good at that."
"Okay. Twenty minutes, not ten. Still faster than before."

qa.q: What date is the annual day actually on?
qa.a: It is on the twelfth.

qa.q: How was Hansa feeling while relying on the AI tool for the newsletter?
qa.a: Hansa was feeling rushed and pressured, with forty copies to print that night, and excited to finish in ten minutes.

qa.q: What rule does Sudha suggest for using AI tools?
qa.a: Check every date, name and quote, and write the personal parts yourself, because you are responsible for what goes out.

qa.q: What would change if Hansa printed the newsletter unchecked?
qa.a: Parents would get the wrong date and a fake quote, which could confuse them and embarrass the principal and Hansa.

grounding: Shows a young teacher learning to verify AI output and keep responsibility for what goes out.

passage: Last spring our firm brought in an AI tool to summarise contracts, and I loved it. What used to take me a morning took twenty minutes. By summer I had stopped reading the full documents at all. Then my senior, Mridul, asked, 'Eshaan, what does the indemnity clause say?' It was in a supplier contract I had 'reviewed'. The summary had skipped it. I hadn't read it. I remember the silence on that call. Nothing bad had happened yet, but it could have, and my name was on the review, not the tool's. Since then I use the summary as a map, not the territory: I read every clause it flags and spot-check the ones it doesn't. Once a week I review one contract fully by hand, so I don't lose the skill. Mridul calls it my gym day. I'm slower than I was in summer. I'm also better.

qa.q: What did the AI summary skip?
qa.a: An indemnity clause in a supplier contract.

qa.q: What did Eshaan feel during the silence on that call?
qa.a: Embarrassed and alarmed, realising Eshaan's name was on a review that had not really been done.

qa.q: How does Eshaan now use the tool responsibly?
qa.a: Eshaan treats summaries as a map, reads the flagged clauses, spot-checks the rest, and reviews one contract fully by hand each week to keep the skill.

qa.q: How might Mridul see Eshaan's weekly 'gym day'?
qa.a: As a sensible habit that keeps the junior sharp and accountable, which is why Mridul jokes about it approvingly.

grounding: A young professional looks back on over-relying on an AI tool and how they now verify its work and protect their own skills.

passage:
Supervisor's note, customer-support pilot (Uday, operations head):
Pallavi, 24, led our trial of an AI assistant for routine customer queries. What stood out was not the speed, though replies went from hours to minutes. It was her caution. Before launch she tested it on two hundred real past queries and found it confidently gave wrong refund rules in about one in ten. She refused to go live until those were fixed. She insisted that every complaint, refund or angry message goes to a human, and that each reply says it came from an assistant. She also kept two team members answering some queries by hand every day, 'so we don't forget how'. One week an agent flagged a wrong answer anyway; Pallavi traced it and shared the fix openly. Next step: I have asked her to write our guidelines for any future AI tools.

qa.q: How many past queries did Pallavi test the assistant on?
qa.a: Two hundred real past queries.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's refusal to go live suggest about what she cared about?
qa.a: She cared more about customers getting correct answers than about launching quickly or showing off speed.

qa.q: Which of Pallavi's safeguards keep humans accountable?
qa.a: Sending complaints, refunds and angry messages to people, labelling assistant replies, keeping staff practising by hand, and tracing errors openly.

qa.q: How does Uday see Pallavi's work?
qa.a: He values her caution over speed and trusts her enough to ask her to write guidelines for future tools.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a young employee deploying an AI assistant responsibly with human oversight and verification.
